Expense Type: Borrowing costs (eg., guarantee fees, bank option fees, prepayment fees, early redemption fees, etc.)
Tax Treatment:
Generally, interest expenses incurred on loans or borrowings taken to finance income-producing assets are tax-deductible.

Borrowing costs are costs other than interest expenses that are incurred to secure lower interest rates on loans or borrowings to finance expenditure that produces taxable income.

To align the tax treatment of borrowing costs with interest expenses, a list of tax-deductible borrowing costs is prescribed in the Income Tax regulations. To qualify for tax deduction, the borrowing costs must be incurred as a substitute for interest expense or to reduce interest costs.

Please refer to the IRAS e-Tax guide for the list of qualifying borrowing cost for more information on tax deduction for borrowing costs other than interest expenses.

Expense Type: Cash top-ups made to your employees' CPF Medisave Accounts
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the cash top-ups are made to employees’ CPF MediSave Accounts on their behalf on or after 1 January 2026.

Not deductible if the cash top-ups are made to employees' CPF MediSave Accounts on their behalf before 1 January 2026.

Expense Type: Cash top-ups made to your employees' CPF Retirement Accounts/ Special Accounts under the Retirement Sum Topping-Up Scheme
Tax Treatment: Tax deductible as cash top-ups made to your employees’ CPF Retirement Accounts/ Special Accounts, on the employees’ behalf under the Retirement Sum Topping-Up Scheme are staff costs.
Tax deductible if the expenses are not entrance fees or transfer fees and are incurred in the production of income.
Tax deductible if the compensation or damages incurred are revenue in nature.
Tax deductible if the expenses are incurred as part of the pre-existing obligations of the employer to the staff. This is regardless of whether there is a complete cessation of business.

Expense Type: Donations made to an approved Institution of a Public Character (IPC)
Tax Treatment:
Donations are not deductible as they are not incurred in the production of income. However, a company may enjoy a 250% tax deduction on qualifying donations made to an Institution of a Public Character (IPC). When donating to IPCs, the company must provide its registration number to the IPCs for the relevant information to be transmitted to IRAS and included in the company’s tax assessment. No tax deduction may be made if the information is not provided to IRAS.

Deductions for qualifying donations are automatically reflected in the company’s tax assessment based on information from the IPC. The company does not need to declare the donation amount in its tax return.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information about donations.

Expense Type: Double tax deduction for internationalisation scheme (DTDI)
Tax Treatment:
Under Sections 14B, 14H and 14I of the Income Tax Act 1947, companies may claim double tax deduction on qualifying expenses incurred for qualifying activities, up to $150,000 per YA until YA 2026. The cap will be increased to $400,000 with effect from YA 2027.

The qualifying activities that do not require prior approval from EnterpriseSG or the Singapore Tourism Board (STB) are:
- Overseas market development trips/ missions
- Overseas investment study trips/ missions
- Overseas trade fairs
- Local trade fairs approved by EnterpriseSG or STB
- Virtual trade fairs approved by EnterpriseSG
- Product/ service certification approved by EnterpriseSG
- Overseas advertising and promotional campaigns
- Design of packaging for overseas markets
- Advertising in local trade publications approved by EnterpriseSG
- Investment feasibility/ due diligence studies#
- Master licensing and franchising#
- Market surveys/ feasibility studies#
- Overseas business development#
- Production of corporate brochures for overseas distribution#

# Qualifying activities from YA 2027.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on the double tax deduction for internationlisation scheme.

Tax deductible if there is a continuation of the existing business. This is because the payments are incurred for the company to continue its income producing activities of the business.

Not deductible where the business completely ceases. This is because such non-contractual retrenchment payments are made gratuitously at the discretion of the company and invariably involve some element of goodwill. Hence, they are not considered wholly and exclusively incurred in the production of income, as the income producing activities of the business will cease.

Expense Type: Expenses incurred before commencement of business
Tax Treatment:
Expenses incurred before business commences its business are not tax-deductible as these are incurred to set up the operations of the business and not wholly and exclusively in the production of income.

A business is treated as having commenced its business on the first day of the basis period in which it earns its first dollar of business receipt (i.e. deemed date of commencement of business). Revenue expenses incurred from the deemed date of commencement of business as well as one year prior to the deemed date of commencement of business are tax-deductible.

Please refer to the IRAS e-Tax guide for more information on the deductibility of expenses incurred before business revenue is earned.

Expense Type: Expenses incurred during vacancy period of lease
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the Comptroller is satisfied that the company has made reasonable efforts to procure a lessee for the immovable property while it is vacant.

Examples of the following expenses on the immovable property that  qualify for tax deduction:
- Repair
- Insurance
- Maintenance or upkeep
- Property tax
Not deductible if the fines or penalties are imposed for the breach of any statute or government regulation.

Tax deductible if the transactions giving rise to the losses are revenue in nature.  

Not deductible if the transactions giving rise to the losses are capital in nature.

Whether the transaction is capital or revenue in nature depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. Companies are encouraged to include a tax schedule in their income tax computation, showing an itemised breakdown of the underlying transactions/ assets/ liabilities that gave rise to the foreign exchange differences. 

Please refer to the IRAS e-Tax guide for a sample breakdown format and for more information about the tax treatment on foreign exchange losses.

Expense Type: Foreign exchange losses arising from designated bank account
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the bank account is maintained solely for revenue purposes in a particular foreign currency or meets the de minimis limit.

Not deductible if the bank account is maintained for mixed purposes. If the company does not wish to track the nature of the transactions within its foreign bank account, the exchange losses arising from the revaluation will be treated as capital in nature and will not be deductible.

Please refer to the IRAS e-Tax guide for more information on the designated bank account and de-minimis limit.

Expense Type: Foreign exchange losses arising from translation
Tax Treatment:
Not deductible as these are merely notional gains or losses.

Please refer to the IRAS e-Tax guide for more information on deductibility of the foreign exchange losses arising from translation.

Expense Type: Foreign registered cars used exclusively outside Singapore
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the car is used for business purposes.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on deductibility of expenses incurred for foreign cars used exclusively outside Singapore.

Expense Type: Group insurance policy with any form of cash surrender or investment/ savings value
Tax Treatment:
Not deductible as the expenses relate to the acquisition of a capital asset (i.e. cash surrender or investment/savings value).

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on deductibility of insurance premiums.

Tax deductible as the premiums are regarded as staff costs where employees are the intended beneficiaries, either because they are the named beneficiaries or because there is a contractual obligation for the employer to pass the payout to the employees or their next of kin. Tax deduction is extended to similar policies where employers are the beneficiaries of the policy and there is no contractual obligation to pass the payout to employees.   

An administrative concession was granted to allow companies to elect not to claim a tax deduction on the group term life insurance premiums paid by the employer if such employment benefits are not taxed on the employees.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on deductibility of insurance premiums.

GST input tax paid/ payable by a company is not deductible if:
- the company is required to register under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1993 (“GSTA)”, but failed to do so; or
- the company is entitled under the GSTA to credit that amount of tax as an input tax.

GST output tax borne by a person registered as a taxable person under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1993 (“GSTA”) is not deductible. As an exception, output tax paid or payable on a reverse charge supply is allowable to the extent the credit of such amount as input tax is not allowed under the GSTA.

Expense Type: Income tax of employee borne by employer
Tax Treatment: Tax deductible if it is in accordance with the employee’s employment contract.

Expense Type: Insurance premium for work injury compensation
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible as the expenses are incurred for the purpose of insuring against the employer’s statutory liability under the Work Injury Compensation Act 2019.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on deductibility of insurance premiums.

Tax deductible if the IP licensing expenditure is incurred to license intellectual property rights (IPRs) for use in the company's business or if used for a qualifying Research and Development (R&D) project.

Under the Enterprise Innovation Scheme (EIS), companies with annual revenue of less than $500 million in the basis period of the YA of claim can qualify for a 300% enhanced tax deduction, up to a combined cap of $400,000 for each YA from YA 2024 to YA 2028. For qualifying IP licensing expenditure incurred in excess of the combined cap of $400,000 for each YA from YA 2024 to YA 2028, companies can claim a 100% tax deduction.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on the EIS scheme for qualifying IP licensing expenditure.

Expense Type: Intellectual Property (IP) Registration costs (i.e. official and professional fees)
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if both the legal and economic ownership of the IP belong to the company. The qualifying costs incurred in registering patents, trademarks, designs and plant varieties (collectively referred to as ‘qualifying intellectual property rights’ or ‘IP’) cover official fees and professional fees.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on the official fees and professional fees incurred in the registration.

Under the Enterprise Innovation Scheme (EIS), companies with annual revenue of less than $500 million in the basis period of the YA of claim can qualify for a 300% enhanced tax deduction, up to a combined cap of $400,000 for each YA from YA 2024 to YA 2028. For qualifying IP licensing expenditure incurred in excess of the combined cap of $400,000 for each YA from YA 2024 to YA 2028, companies can claim a 100% tax deduction.

Expense Type: Interest expenses on loan for general working capital purposes
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the loan is used to purchase income producing assets. 

However, if the company wants to claim a tax deduction but cannot identify and track the use of the interest bearing working capital loan, the Total Asset Method (TAM) is used to determine the interest expense attributable to non-income producing assets, for which tax deduction is not allowed.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on the TAM calculation method.

Expense Type: Interest expenses on loans or borrowings specifically taken up to finance income producing assets
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the company is able to substantiate that the interest-bearing loan is taken to fund a specific income-producing asset.

Some examples are:
- Properties that derive rental income and are not vacant 
- Interest bearing loans

Please refer to the IRAS e-Tax guide for more information on deductibility of interest expense.

Expense Type: Interest incurred on loans to re-finance prior loan
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the re-financing loan is a revenue loan (i.e. a loan taken solely to repay an existing loan that was entered into for revenue purpose).

Where the re-financing loan is a capital loan (i.e. taken solely to repay an existing loan that was entered into for a capital purpose), the deductibility of the interest expense incurred on the re-financing loan follows that of the repaid loan based on the direct link test: 
- If interest deductions were previously allowed on the repaid loan, the interest expense on the re-financing loan is accorded similar interest deductions. 
- If the interest expense incurred on the repaid loan was subject to adjustments under the Total Asset Method (TAM), TAM similarly applies to the re-financing loan. If the interest expense on the repaid loan was not tax deductible, the interest expense on the re-financing loan is similarly not tax deductible.

For instances where a re-financing loan is not used solely to repay an existing loan (e.g. the principal amount of the re-financing loan obtained is higher than the principal of the existing loan and the balance is used for other purposes), the deductibility of the interest expense on the portion of re-financing loan not used to repay the existing loan is determined by the purpose of the additional loan amount (i.e. whether it is for a revenue or capital use).

Tax deductible if all of the following conditions are met:

(a) The purpose of the policy is to insure the company against loss of profits arising from the death or disability of a “keyman”.
(b) The capital sum insured is directly related to the extent of the annual profits directly attributable to the services of the “keyman”.
(c) The insurance policy remains the property of the company, and there must not be any assignment of the benefits under the policy to the insured or the insured’s family.
(d) The insurance policy does not provide for a cash surrender or investment value.
(e) The loss of the “keyman” does not affect the company’s entire profit-making structure.

Please refer to the IRAS e-Tax guide for more information on deductibility of keyman insurance premiums.

Tax deductible if the interest arising from the late payment is in the nature of a contractual obligation and does not constitute a fine or penalty imposed for breaching the law, and that it is incurred wholly and exclusively in the production of income. 

Examples of deductible late payment interest: 
- Late interest or fine on management fees to a Management Corporation for a Strata Title Plan (“MCST”)
- Late interest on loan repayments on credit facilities to a financial institution, if it is incurred wholly and exclusively in the production of income

Examples of non-deductible late payment interest: 
- Late interest on Central Provident Fund (“CPF”) contributions
- Late interest or fine on management fees to a MCST that is imposed under section 40(10) of the Building Maintenance and Strata Management Act (“BMSMA”)
Tax deductible if the expense is incurred in the production of income and not prohibited under the Income Tax Act 1947.

Tax deductible if it is a recurring licence fees or subscription costs and are incurred in the production of income. If it is a one-time purchase or perpetual licence, it is considered as a capital expense and not deductible, though capital allowances may be claimable instead.
Tax deductible if the losses occurred despite the company having put in place a sufficient system of checks and balances, and the employees do not have overriding power or control.

Expense Type: Losses through theft or burglary in business premises
Tax Treatment: Tax deductible if the losses are revenue in nature and incidental to the company.

Tax deductible, but capped at 1% of the total employee remuneration accrued for the year. The cap increases to 2% if the company implements/provides any of the following:
(i) Portable Medical Benefits Scheme (PMBS) 
(ii) Transferable Medical Insurance Scheme (TMIS) 
(iii) Inpatient medical insurance benefits in the form of portable medical shield plans

Medical expense include:
- Maternity health care
- Natal care
- Preventive and therapeutic treatment expense
- Provision of a medical clinic by the employer
- Cash allowance in lieu of medical expense
- Dental expense
- Premium incurred on medical and dental insurance
- Contributions made by a company to the employees' CPF MediSave accounts
- Medical expense incurred for employees' spouse and children

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on deductibility of medical expenses.

Tax deductible if the expenses are incurred for goods and commercial vehicles. Motor vehicle expenses incurred on private cars (e.g. S-plated cars) and business cars (e.g. Q-plated and RU-plated cars registered on or after 1 Apr 1998) are not deductible. This applies to expenses paid in the form of reimbursement even if the cars are used for business purposes. 

Some examples of goods and commercial vehicles are:
- Van
- Lorry
- Bus

Some examples of motor vehicle expenses are:
- Parking fees
- Petrol cost
- Repairs
- Maintenance

Payments for transportation services (i.e. payments for services to commute from one place to another without the passenger having any control or possession of the motor car) are deductible if incurred for business purposes. In contrast, expenses incurred on hiring a private car and the operation or maintenance of a hired private car are not deductible unless the company is carrying on the business of hiring out cars or providing driving instruction.

Tax deductible if there is a continuation of the existing business, as the expenses are incurred by the employer for the welfare of the employees as part of their continuing income producing activities and are considered wholly and exclusively incurred in the production of income.

Not deductible if there is a complete cessation of business.

For a specific provision that is revenue in nature, no deduction is allowed unless there is already a legal liability to pay at the time of accrual and the amount of provision is reasonably estimated. Examples of specific provisions that are deductible at the time of accrual are the specific provisions for stock obsolescence and bad/doubtful debts. 

For a general provision that is revenue in nature, no deduction is allowed at the time of accrual but deduction will be allowed when the expenses is incurred, usually upon utilisation of the provision or when the legal liability to pay crystallises.

Tax deductible if it is incurred for business purposes. However, if the expenses relate to the use of private (e.g. S-plated cars) or business cars (e.g. Q-plated and RU-plated cars registered on or after 1 Apr 1998). Such expenses are specifically prohibited under the Income Tax Act 1947 even if the cars are used for business purposes.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on deductibility of reimbursement to employees for transport expenses.

Expense Type: Reimbursement of expenses for overtime transport
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the expenses are meant for working beyond official working hours (i.e. working before or after official working hours on normal workdays, or working on off days, weekends and public holidays) on an ad hoc basis, and such payment policy is generally available to all staff.

Some examples of expenses for overtime transport are:
- Tax trips
- Private hire car services through mobile applications between home and office

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on the deductibility of reimbursement to employees for transport expenses.

Expense Type: Reimbursement of expenses for travel between home and airport for overseas business trips
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the expenses do not relate to the use of private (e.g. S-plated cars)  or business cars (e.g. Q-plated and RU-plated cars registered on or after 1 Apr 1998). Such expenses are specifically prohibited under the Income Tax Act 1947 even if the cars are used for business purposes.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on the deductibility of reimbursement to employees for transport expenses.

Expense Type: Reimbursement of expenses for travel between home and workplace
Tax Treatment:
Not deductible as these are personal trips for ordinary commuting to the workplace. 

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on deductibility of reimbursement to employees for transport expenses.

Expense Type: Reimbursement of transport expenses for discharging official duties
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the expenses do not relate to the use of private (e.g. S-plated cars) or business cars (e.g. Q-plated and RU-plated cars registered on or after 1 Apr 1998). Such expenses are specifically prohibited under the Income Tax Act 1947 even if the cars are used for business purposes.

Some examples of transport expenses for discharging official duties are:
- Travelling from office to meet a client
- Travelling between home and external venues for business meetings
- Travelling from the place of one client to another.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on deductibility of reimbursement to employees for transport expenses.

Not deductible, as reinstatement costs are considered capital expenses incurred in respect of the company's premises that have been vacated and are no longer used for acquiring income. 

However, reinstatement costs qualifies for tax deduction when the: 

(i) cost claimed do not relate to any provisions made under the Financial Reporting Standard (FRS) 16 (i.e. the expense has been incurred); 
(ii) cost claimed are contractually provided for in the tenancy agreement ; and
(iii) premises are not vacated due to any cessation of business

Note: Under paragraph 16 of FRS 16, the cost of an item of property, plant and equipment includes the initial estimate of the costs of dismantling and removing the item and restoring the site on which the item is located, the obligation for which an entity incurs either when the item is acquired or as a consequence of having used the item during a particular period for purposes other than to produce inventories during that period.

Tax deductible if the premise is occupied for business purposes.

If only part of the premise is used for business purposes, only the rental expense specifically attributable to that area is deductible. Apportionment of expense is not allowed unless the expense can be clearly identified as related to business purposes. 

The company is required to maintain proper documentation to support the claim for the portion of rental expense incurred for income producing activities. This includes detailed records demonstrating the specific area of the premise used for business purposes.

Tax deductible if the expenses are incurred in the production of income. These expenses should not be subject to a capital allowance claim under Section 19 or Section 19A of the Income Tax Act 1947 and should not be incurred for reconstruction or rebuilding of any premises, buildings, structures or works of a permanent nature.

Expense Type: Sponsorship (eg. payment made to advertise sponsor's goods and services)
Tax Treatment: Tax deductible if these are payments made by the sponsor to advertise the sponsor's goods and services whether in the form of money, goods or services and are incurred in the production of income. The payments should not be private or capital in nature.

Tax deductible if incurred in the production of income. Whether a staff benefit is taxable to an employee does not automatically determine whether the business can claim a tax deduction on that staff benefit.

Tax deductible if the statutory and regulatory expenses are incurred to:
(a) comply with any written law of Singapore or another country/ territory
(b) comply with any code, standard, rule, requirement or other document issued by any government or public authority or by a securities exchange
(c) study the impact of any proposed law/ document
(d) prevent or detect any non-compliance with any law/ document
(e) voluntarily comply with any law/ document

Some examples of tax deductible statutory and regulatory expenses are:
- Accounting fees
- Audit fees
- Secretarial fees

Some examples of statutory and regulatory expenses that are not deductible are:
- Incorporation fees
- Striking-off fees
- Liquidation fees

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on statutory and regulatory expenses.
Tax deductible as contributions made to SRS accounts on employees’ behalf are staff costs, subject to the annual SRS contribution cap for each employee.

Tax deductible if the expenses are incurred in the production of income.

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information on deductibility of transport allowance to staff.

Expense Type: Upfront expenses incurred in obtaining, renewing or extending leases
Tax Treatment:
Tax deductible if the property is used for business purposes and the conditions under Section 14ZE of the Income Tax Act 1947 are met.  

Some examples of upfront expense are:  
- Commission
- Legal fee
- Stamp duty
- Advertising expenses

Upfront expenses incurred for any of the following is not deductible under Section 14ZE of the Income Tax Act 1947:
(i) any leases or any renewal or extension of lease for a term that (excluding any option for the renewal or extension of the lease) exceed 3 years;
(ii) any acquisition, grant, novation, transfer or assignment (however described) of a lease due to acquisition, sale, transfer or restructuring of any business; or
(iii) a lease under an arrangement where the immovable property is sold by and leased back to the seller of the immovable property

Not deductible, as a website qualifies as plant and machinery. Companies may claim capital allowances under Section 19A(10) of the Income Tax Act 1947 on the development or purchase costs of a website over one year.

Expense Type: Withholding tax payment borne by the local payer on behalf of a Non-Residents, where the contract is silent on who bears the withholding tax
Tax Treatment:
For withholding tax on interest payments borne by local payer: 
- Where the loan is revenue in nature, the withholding tax borne will be deductible if it is wholly and exclusively incurred in the production of income. 
- Where the loan is capital in nature,  the withholding tax borne will be deductible only if the withholding tax forms part of the gross contractual interest amount. Where the local payer bears the withholding tax on behalf of the non-resident, the withholding tax is not deductible as it does not qualify as interest under Section 14(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act 1947 and is prohibited under Section 15(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act 1947 as capital expenditure. 

For withholding tax on other payments (e.g. royalty, service fees, etc.) borne by local payer, it will be deductible if it is incurred wholly and exclusively in the production of income. 

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information about deductibility of withholding tax on interest payment.

Expense Type: Withholding tax payment for which the local payer is contractually liable to bear on behalf of Non-Residents
Tax Treatment:
For withholding tax on interest payments borne by local payer: 
- Where the loan is revenue in nature, the withholding tax borne will be deductible as part of the interest payment if it is wholly and exclusively incurred in the production of income. 
- Where the loan is capital in nature,  the withholding tax borne will be deductible as part of the interest payment if the interest is payable on capital employed in acquiring income. 

For withholding tax on other payments (e.g. royalty, service fees, etc.) borne by local payer, it will be deductible as part of the underlying payment if it is incurred wholly and exclusively in the production of income. 

Please refer to the IRAS website for more information about deductibility of withholding tax on interest payment.
